title: A Busy Product Page
statement: A shop's product page gets 5,000 reads per second at peak. The database can serve about 1,000 reads per second and cannot be upgraded this quarter. Product details change a few times a day, and a price that is up to 60 seconds old is acceptable. A test with a warm cache measured a hit rate of about 90% with a 55-second TTL, with or without deleting entries on the few daily changes, and every database read, including storing the result in the cache, finishes within 2 seconds. Which read path fits best?
examples: Most reads ask for a few hundred popular products
A price change must reach users within 60 seconds
constraints: The database stays at about 1,000 reads per second
Data may be up to 60 seconds old
A slow read can store a value up to 2 seconds old

approaches.name: Read every request from the database and add more servers in front of it
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.time: All 5,000 reads per second reach the database
approaches.why: More servers only send more reads to the same database, which can serve about 1,000 per second. The bottleneck stays.

approaches.name: Cache-aside with a 55-second TTL, and delete the cache entry on every change
approaches.label: best
approaches.time: Hits ≈1 ms; at a 90% hit rate, 5,000 × 0.1 = 500 database reads per second
approaches.why: Most reads become hits, so the database stays within its limit. Deleting on change shows new prices at once in the usual case, and because a value can be at most 55 + 2 = 57 seconds old even in a race with a slow read, the 60-second rule always holds.

approaches.name: Cache-aside with a 55-second TTL and no delete on change
approaches.label: valid
approaches.time: Same measured hit rate, about 90%: 500 database reads per second
approaches.why: This meets both requirements: a value is at most 55 + 2 = 57 seconds old. It is simpler, but users see the old price for up to 57 seconds after every change, which deleting on change avoids in the usual case.

approaches.name: Cache-aside with no TTL and no delete
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.space: Memory grows with every product read
approaches.why: A changed price would never leave the cache, which breaks the 60-second rule.

title: Showing an Account Balance
statement: A banking app shows a user's account balance. Right after a transfer, the balance on screen must be exact. Balance reads are about 300 per second, and the database serves them easily. The profile name and settings shown next to the balance change rarely. What should the team cache?
examples: A user sends money and opens the balance screen one second later
constraints: The balance must be exact right after a change
The database has plenty of capacity for 300 reads per second

approaches.name: Cache the balance with a 5-minute TTL
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: A user could see the old balance for up to 5 minutes after a transfer, which breaks the first requirement.

approaches.name: Read the balance from the database; cache only the rarely changing profile name and settings
approaches.hint: Cache what can be a little old
approaches.label: best
approaches.time: Balance read from the database, settings ≈1 ms
approaches.why: The balance is always exact, and the database has capacity for it. Caching the rarely changing parts still saves work where slightly old data is harmless.

approaches.name: Do not cache anything on this screen
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: This meets both requirements, because the database handles 300 reads per second easily. It gives up a small saving on the settings that could safely be cached.

title: Product Images Around the World
statement: A shop with its servers in Virginia, USA, sells worldwide. Product photos are 200 to 500 KB each, the same for every user, and change only when a seller uploads a new photo. Measurements for users in Asia: the round trip to Virginia is about 230 ms, the origin server answers a photo request in about 50 ms and is only 20% busy, and CDN edge servers in Asian cities are about 20–50 ms away. Requirements: each photo must start arriving within 200 ms of the browser asking for it, and after a seller uploads a new photo, product pages loaded more than an hour later must show it. Product pages are built by the servers for each request and are never cached on the CDN. How should the photos be served?
examples: A user in Hanoi opens a product page with 8 photos
constraints: Each photo starts arriving within 200 ms for users in Asia
Pages loaded more than an hour after an upload show the new photo
Photos are the same for every user

approaches.name: Move the photos to a faster server in Virginia
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.time: Each photo still crosses the ocean
approaches.why: The origin is only 20% busy, so a faster server saves little. Every photo request still needs at least one 230 ms round trip to Virginia, which already breaks the 200 ms requirement.

approaches.name: Serve photos through a CDN with a TTL of one hour
approaches.label: valid
approaches.time: Nearby edge when it has a copy
approaches.why: This meets all requirements: photos come from an edge 20–50 ms away, and after an hour an edge's copy has expired, so the next request for that photo asks the origin and gets the new one. Unchanged photos may only need to be confirmed, but every hour each edge still asks the origin about every popular photo.

approaches.name: Serve photos through a CDN with a long TTL, and give every new photo a new file name
approaches.hint: A new name means a new copy
approaches.label: best
approaches.time: Nearby edge for almost every photo
approaches.why: Photos come from a nearby edge. A new upload gets a new file name, for example photo-42-v2.jpg, which is a new key at the CDN, and the product page, built fresh for each request, links to it at once, so the one-hour rule holds easily. Edges rarely need to ask the origin about unchanged photos.

approaches.name: Keep the photos in the Virginia server's memory
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: This removes disk reads in Virginia, but each request still needs at least one 230 ms round trip, so the 200 ms requirement is still broken for users in Asia.
